rationale: THE CLOSEST C++ CONSTRUCT TO `decorates`, MEASURED. The canonical contract (src/ast/types.ts, Decorates) is 'a decorator is APPLIED TO a declaration ... the runtime applies it while the declaration is created'. C++ has no such construct: attributes are COMPILER METADATA, and even when an attribute's argument list carries a CALL expression the call is evaluated inside the attribute's own grammar, nothing is applied to the declaration, and no decorator value exists. The analyzer emits both near-misses as what they are: `calls` (attribute-argument calls `aligned(16)` and `compute(1)` become calls edges from the file scope). RULED on LANGUAGE semantics, not grammar: this fixture PINS the mapping that would be wrong if `decorates` were ever emitted for an attribute.

expectSymbols.name: logf
expectSymbols.note: attribute-decorated declaration; an attribute exists, a decorator does not.

expectSymbols.name: Aligned
expectSymbols.note: GNU attribute spelling on a class head.

expectSymbols.name: compute
expectSymbols.note: declared so the attribute-argument call PARSES as a call.

expectSymbols.name: annotated
expectSymbols.note: `annotate(compute(1))`: a call expression INSIDE an attribute — still not a decorator application.

expectRelationships.note: the GNU-attribute argument is call-shaped; it is emitted as `calls`, the honest value.
a call inside an attribute argument list is a CALL; `decorates` would claim the declaration is decorated by it, which C++ does not say.

forbidRelationships.note: NO `decorates` row may exist for any attribute form — the value's contract requires a decorator applied to a declaration at run time, which the language does not spell.
the near-miss target must never become a decorator.
